summary: Round 3. The round-2 MAJOR is genuinely closed: measured exhaustively over every Unicode code point in both string fields (4,448,776 accepted values, plus adjacent-surrogate pairs, numeric extremes, codec-marker lookalikes and 4000-char values) there is now NO value the constructor accepts whose encode/decode round trip is not identity, and no re-encode that differs byte-for-byte. Separately fuzzed decode over ~1.02M corrupt inputs -- every single-byte truncation, substitution and deletion of a valid encoding plus 1M random/mutated buffers -- and zero unchecked exceptions escaped the throws IOException contract, so the round-2 decode(null) and truncated-mid-string findings are closed too. F5 (javadoc carrying a refuted defence) is fixed and the replacement text is accurate. F4 is fixed: the M4 SPEC table now carries separate M4.3 and M4.3b rows, they agree with backlog.md, and no other document in docs/ references M4.3 at all. F8 is NOT fixed -- the staged backlog row still says 'All 11 mutation verified' against a 21-test file. Five minors, none blocking; the two that matter are a measured-false justification comment reproduced in three places, and a decode-side survivor of the exact mechanism the round-2 MAJOR closed on the encode side.

findings.title: F8 was reported fixed but the staged bytes still say 'All 11 mutation verified' against a 21-test file
findings.failure_scenario: The staged M4.3 row -- the row this commit marks `done`, and the permanent record of what was verified -- reads 'All 11 mutation verified'. `git show :format/src/test/java/binjava/format/LeaseTest.java | grep -c '@Test'` returns 21. The number was raised in rounds 1 and 2 as tests were added, and the row was never updated. A reader auditing this task later counts 21 tests, reads that 11 were mutation-verified, and cannot tell which 10 were not -- so the row understates the work AND leaves the mutation status of ten tests unstated, which is the one thing a `done` row exists to record. It also fails the internal cross-check the row itself invites: the suite total 453 = 432 (M4.2's stated total) + 21, so 21 is derivable from two other numbers in the same document while the row says 11. Fix is one character in one cell; per rule 11 it belongs in the commit body or the milestone-boundary harvest rather than a round 4.

findings.title: The stated reason for choosing the code-point range over Character::isSurrogate is false, and is reproduced in three places
findings.failure_scenario: The comment says Character::isSurrogate 'takes a `char`, and casting a code point down to one truncates every astral character into the surrogate range, refusing valid emoji'. MEASURED: of the 1,048,576 astral code points, `Character.isSurrogate((char) cp)` is true for 32,768 of them -- 3.13%, not 'every'. And U+1F600, the exact emoji LeaseTest uses at the assertion that is supposed to demonstrate the difference, casts to U+F600 (Private Use Area), for which isSurrogate is FALSE: the rejected alternative would not have refused it. Consequence, measured by building the mutant `codePoints().anyMatch(cp -> Character.isSurrogate((char) cp))` and running the three assertions of anUnpairedSurrogateIsRefusedThoughAValidAstralPairIsNot against it: all three pass. The test written to defend this design choice does not discriminate between the choice and the alternative it names, so the mutation that motivates the whole comment survives. The mutant does introduce a real bug -- a podId containing U+1D800 is wrongly refused -- but nothing in the suite sees it. The chosen implementation is CORRECT; only its justification is wrong. The same false claim appears verbatim in LeaseTest.java's comment on that test and in the backlog M4.3 row ('would truncate every astral character, refusing valid emoji'), which is the duplicate-copies failure mode the M4.0 row already names as recurring. Accurate replacement: `Character::isSurrogate` takes a `char`, so it must be reached either by casting a code point (which is lossy and misses most astral characters) or by iterating `chars()` (which sees BOTH halves of a valid pair as surrogates and so refuses every astral character); the code-point range avoids both.

findings.title: The round-2 lossy-conversion mechanism is closed on the encode side only: decode silently repairs invalid UTF-8 and the canonical check cannot see it
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the unmutated staged code. Take `new Lease(7, "pod1", "e", 5L).encode()` and set the byte holding the '1' of "pod1" to 0xFF -- a byte no UTF-8 sequence can begin. `Lease.decode` ACCEPTS it and returns holderPodId="pod\uFFFD"; `back.encode()` does not equal the bytes that were stored. This is exactly the mechanism of the round-2 MAJOR -- `new String(bytes, UTF_8)` at :172 is lossy, and the canonical comparison at :199 compares `parsed.encode()` against `s.getBytes(UTF_8)`, i.e. against the RE-encoding of the already-lossy string rather than against the raw bytes, so both sides derive from the same conversion and the loss is invisible. The round-2 fix closed the encode direction (constructor refuses unpaired surrogates); the decode direction was left open. Operational consequence: `ctl/lease/<slot>.json` is the object this format is justified by being hand-editable -- an operator editing it in a non-UTF-8 locale, or a stray byte from any tool, yields a lease that decodes to a holder identity nobody wrote. A pod comparing holderPodId against its own POD_NAME gets false and takes over a lease it may already hold; a pod renewing writes the U+FFFD-mangled podId back under putIfMatch, which succeeds, silently rewriting the recorded holder. Blast radius is bounded to a failover rather than a split brain, because the epoch is ASCII digits and untouched and safety rests on the epoch in the object path (the class javadoc says so) -- which is why this is minor and not major, and why it needs an already-corrupt object to trigger. It also falsifies decode's own javadoc at :157, 'REFUSES anything that is not exactly this shape, loudly and now': non-UTF-8 bytes are not that shape and are not refused. Remedy is one line and does not change the format -- compare against the stripped RAW bytes at :199, or decode with a CharsetDecoder set to REPORT. Belongs in a backlog row, not a round 4.

findings.title: F7 still open: the unpaired-surrogate message names the field twice and never says where or what
findings.failure_scenario: `field + " may not contain an unpaired surrogate: " + field` prints e.g. `holderPodId may not contain an unpaired surrogate: holderPodId`. The colon leads an operator to expect the offending value or position and delivers the field name again. Eleven lines above, the control-character branch gets this right -- `holderPodId[3]=0xd800` -- so the two rejections from the same method behave differently for no reason. An operator whose pod name was rejected at startup cannot tell WHICH character to remove from the message alone. Judged against rule 11: leaving it is the right call. It is cosmetic, the fix would add prose that becomes the next round's review surface, and this task is already past rule 12's two-round cap; it should be harvested at the milestone boundary under rule 13 rather than fixed here.

findings.title: The no-version-field flag day is recorded only in a code comment, not in the M4.8 row that will choose to trigger it
findings.failure_scenario: Judging the question as asked: refusing unknown fields is the RIGHT call for M4 and should not change here -- with no version field, an older reader silently discarding a field is strictly worse than refusing, there is no deployed version to be compatible with, and adding a version field now would be inventing a decision M4.3b and M4.5 have not asked for. But the consequence is recorded only inside decode's comment at Lease.java:191-197, which states the behaviour ('an older reader must refuse what it cannot account for') and not the deployment cost. Meanwhile SPEC.md:288 and the M4.8 backlog row at :225 both list 'a pointer in the lease object' as a live candidate M4.8 may choose, each with a stated downside, and neither says that choosing it is now a flag day: a pod running M4.3's decoder that reads a lease written by an upgraded pod throws IOException 'lease is not in canonical form' and cannot learn who holds the lease at all, so during a rolling upgrade the un-upgraded half of the fleet can neither renew nor recognise a valid holder and will attempt takeover against an object it cannot parse. That is a leadership outage on the one object leadership depends on, and it is the kind of fact the M4.0 row already records as being lost by living in one copy. Where it should go: one clause on the M4.8 backlog row's candidate list next to the existing downside for that candidate ('...and, since Lease has no version field and decode refuses unknown fields, adding it is a flag day for every un-upgraded pod'), and the ADR M4.8 is already mandated to write should carry the same. No change to this commit's code is implied.
